en: The Sūtra of the Heart Dhāraṇī of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with the Blue Neck.
At that time, in the palace of King Vaiśravaṇa, the World-Honored One spoke of the past causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara:
"In the past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named..."

Upon observing and contemplating the Tathāgata, who had already attained the path of Buddhahood and remained for twenty-seven days preaching the Dharma, there was at that time a devaputra named Vajranārāyaṇabala.
When the time for his parinirvāṇa approached, this devaputra appeared.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke this heart-mantra of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with the Blue Neck for him.
As soon as that devaputra heard it, he attained the samādhi of Great Compassion and made this vow:
"May all sentient beings who encounter fear or calamity and hear my name be freed from suffering and attain liberation, and may they swiftly realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
"It would be better to recite the name of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara even once than to recite the names of hundreds of thousands of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
At that time, the World-Honored One further addressed the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, saying:

"You should know that after my parinirvāṇa, this son of heaven shall circulate this heart-mantra, extensively perform the work of a Buddha, benefit boundless sentient beings, and establish them on the path to unsurpassed bodhi."
The dhāraṇī says:

"According to tradition, whenever entering the maṇḍala, one should first kneel with lowered body, repent, and make vows; then, sitting in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), one should immediately form the mudrā for purifying the three karmas and practice the mantra. Next, having formed the mudrās for protecting the body of the three families, one should then form the subsequent root mudrā, recite the mantra seven times, and release the mudrā upon the crown of the head."
"However, one should hold the *maṇi* [jewel], whether it be a hundred or a thousand, according to the prescribed time.
The Tripiṭaka Master and Śramaṇa of Daxingshan Monastery, Amoghavajra, by Imperial Decree, annotated and explained the meaning:
*Namo ratnatrayāya*. Homage to the Three Jewels. *Namo āryāvalokiteśvarāya bodhisattvāya*. Homage to the Noble Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
O Mahāsattva! O Mahākāruṇika! You who possess great compassion, you are the severer of all bonds (*sarvabandhanacchedaka*).

You are the one who can exhaust the ocean of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) and all the sufferings of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and you are the one who brings about the pacification of all misfortunes (*sarvamīḍhapraśamana*).
He also causes all diseases to cease: *sarvārti-praśamana-karaḥ*. He can sever all calamities and transgressions:
*sarva-pāya-śodhanaḥ*. He rescues from fear: *trāyate bhayebhyaḥ*. Homage to him!
To the Noble Avalokiteśvara, I now pay homage. *Namo bhagavate āryāvalokiteśvarāya*. I now pay homage to that Holy Avalokiteśvara.

Hail! (110) Next, the method for painting the image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara with the Blue Neck shall be explained.
This image has three faces:
the central face in front displays an expression of compassion and serene joy; the right side is a lion’s face; and the left side is a boar’s face.
He wears a jeweled crown upon his head, within which is the manifested Amitāyus Buddha.
Furthermore, he has four arms: the first right arm holds a staff, the second holds a lotus stalk; the first left arm holds a wheel, and the second holds a conch shell.
He wears a skirt made of tiger skin and a black deer skin draped over the corner of his left shoulder; he is clad in a black snake as a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
Standing upon an eight-petaled lotus, his body is adorned with the radiance of necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and girdles; the sacred thread descends from the corner of his left shoulder.
As for the seal of the Blue-Necked One (*Nīlakaṇṭha*):

with the two hands joined palm-to-palm externally, insert the left thumb into the palm; extend the right thumb straight upward; form the two middle fingers into the shape of lotus petals; extend the two ring fingers straight upward; and cross the two little fingers, pressing the left over the right and extending them upward.

This was completed during the first half of the seventh lunar month in the second year of the Kan’en era (1749), the Ji-si year. Later, Chōtoku obtained an excellent manuscript and collated it, ensuring its ultimate perfection!
